questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Two options presented as the whole field
questions.learningObjective: Identify a choice framed as exhaustive when alternatives were never tested
questions.stem: A transit board hears a new tram line or a bus-only corridor, and the briefing calls these the only two ways forward.

options.text: Neither option is exhaustive; the framing leaves out untested schemes that could meet the need more cheaply
Two workable options make a fair comparison, so the choice is already properly limited
options.misconception: Assumes two workable options make a fair and complete comparison

options.text: Framing two options carefully makes the comparison between them more objective
options.misconception: Believes careful framing removes the need to survey other options

options.text: An even split between tram and bus shows the board has no reason to prefer either
options.misconception: Treats a close comparison as evidence that neither option is fit

questions.explanation: Presenting two workable options can hide untested alternatives. Listing two shows that two are workable, not that others are absent, so the framing itself carries the burden.
questions.hint: Ask which schemes were screened out before the choice.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Circular argument
questions.learningObjective: Expose a conclusion that depends on itself for support

stimulus.body: A depot supervisor argues that the night service should be cut because few passengers use it after ten o'clock, and justifies that low usage by saying passengers have no alternative once the night service is cut.

questions.stem: Which criticism best captures the problem with the supervisor's memo to the transit board?

options.text: A low passenger count reported by a depot is likely to understate demand for the whole network
options.misconception: Assumes a low count is wrong whenever a depot supplies it

options.text: The memo gives no indication of how many night journeys are made by passengers who need them
options.misconception: Treats the absence of a need measure as the central fault

options.text: The usage figure depends on the very cut being argued for, so the argument cannot support its own case
Cutting a service late at night harms shift workers, which the memo should have considered directly
options.misconception: Treats a harm to one group as decisive against the whole proposal

questions.explanation: The premise and the conclusion restate each other: usage is low because the service is cut, and the service should be cut because usage is low. Such an argument adds no information a reader can check.
questions.hint: Ask whether the premise would survive if the cut were rejected.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Generalising from too small a base
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a small sample cannot support a broad conclusion and propose a fix
questions.stem: A route survey of 14 weekday passengers is used to justify a network-wide fare change for the whole region. Explain the flaw and how you would repair it.

answer.exemplar: The sample is far too small and too narrow to support a regional conclusion, since fourteen riders seen on one route cannot represent the mix of trip types, times and purposes across a whole network. The repair is to widen the evidence base before the argument is made: survey a representative spread of routes, days and times, weight the results if some trips are overrepresented, and present the finding with the limits of the sample stated openly.

questions.explanation: A 14-person sample on one route cannot represent a whole network, so the conclusion outruns the evidence. Widening the survey across routes and times restores the link between data and claim.
questions.hint: Ask how many kinds of journey the sample covers.

options.misconception: Assumes an expert verdict transfers across places without conditions

options.text: The endorsement settles the matter because the group named is respected in the industry

Overseas endorsement cannot apply because the conditions in this country are always different
options.misconception: Assumes a foreign scheme can never apply to local conditions

questions.explanation: An appeal to authority holds where the authority is independent and its reasoning is open to checking. Praise for a design in general does not show this scheme meets local need.
questions.hint: Ask whether the endorser judged this scheme or a general idea.

Waiting times must have improved first because the interchange could not work while they were long
options.misconception: Assumes the first effect must come from the newest change

options.misconception: Believes a before-and-after comparison settles the cause

questions.learningObjective: Rewrite a vague claim so that evidence could settle it

questions.stem: The board asks you to redraft the proposal so the claim can be tested. Which revision does that?

options.text: Replace the general phrase with a more enthusiastic one that better conveys the ambition
options.misconception: Adds a stronger adjective so the promise sounds more persuasive

options.text: Specify the measure, the baseline and the date so that later figures could confirm or refute the claim
Name the contractor so that the claim becomes attributable to a named organisation
options.misconception: Names the contractor so the claim becomes attributable to someone

options.text: Delete the commitment entirely so that no later report can dispute what was promised
options.misconception: Removes the claim entirely so no one can later dispute it

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Two options presented as the whole field
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to substantiate a claim that alternatives were ruled out
questions.stem: A route consultation offers two timetable options and reports the alternatives as impractical without cost data. Explain what the report should have done.

answer.exemplar: The report dismisses every alternative on grounds it never demonstrates, and a reader cannot tell whether they were costed, scoped or genuinely ruled out. It should set out the alternatives it examined, give the evidence that eliminated each one and the criteria it applied, so that the board can see whether the two retained options really are the whole field of realistic choices.

questions.explanation: Calling alternatives impractical without showing the evidence invites the reader to take the field as genuinely narrow. The report should show what was ruled out, on what criteria and with what figures.
questions.hint: Ask for the criteria used to rule alternatives out.

options.misconception: Believes poor ranking proves passengers have lost confidence

options.misconception: Accepts the result because a large majority settles the matter

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Sequence mistaken for cause
questions.learningObjective: Explain why coincident timing fails to establish a cause
questions.stem: A depot reports that reliability improved in the same month a new maintenance contract began. Explain why this does not establish that the contract caused the change.

answer.exemplar: Two things began in the same month, so their timings cannot be separated: the improvement might owe as much to a fleet refurbishment or to milder weather as to the new contract. To establish cause, the depot would need evidence that isolates the contract, such as the same period before and after at depots that kept their previous arrangements, or a stated mechanism by which the contract alone should have changed reliability.

questions.explanation: Coincidence in timing is consistent with several causes, so the observation narrows nothing. Evidence from comparable depots that kept the old contract would isolate the effect.
questions.hint: Ask what else began at the same time.

options.text: A general statement that the rebuild will be judged against the best practice of the day

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: When an appeal to authority holds
questions.learningObjective: Identify a missing independence in an expert endorsement and propose a remedy
questions.stem: A board relies on an engineer's assurance that the footbridge is safe, without noting that he designed it. Explain what is missing and how to correct it.

answer.exemplar: The assurance comes from someone with a stake in the outcome, so its value depends on whether his expertise was used to check the work he built rather than to defend it. The correction is to have the calculations independently reviewed by a qualified engineer who has no connection to the design, and to record that review in the paper so that readers can weigh the opinion properly.

questions.explanation: Testimony from an interested party is weaker than testimony from an independent one, and the paper should flag the interest rather than pass the opinion on unexamined. An independent review restores its force.
questions.hint: Ask who benefits if the assurance is believed.

questions.learningObjective: Break a self-supporting pair of claims by importing independent evidence
questions.stem: A councillor says the scheme is affordable because it will pay for itself, and that it will pay for itself because it is affordable. Explain the problem and how to break it.

answer.exemplar: Each claim is being used as the premise for the other, so the pair supports nothing beyond itself and cannot be checked against anything a reader can see. answer.exemplar: A trade body's standard carries weight only if it was drawn up independently of the firms bidding, if its requirements are relevant to the service being bought, and if the paper shows how the proposed contract meets each requirement rather than asserting compliance in general terms. questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: When an appeal to authority holds
questions.learningObjective: Set out how to weigh a professional body's opinion as evidence
questions.stem: A report treats a professional body's view as decisive on a question of engineering standards. Explain how a reader should weigh it.

answer.exemplar: A professional body's view is strong evidence where the question falls squarely inside its expertise, its reasoning is published, and the body has no financial stake in the outcome. It carries less weight where the question has been taken out of its usual remit, the reasons are withheld, or the same firms whose products would be bought also sit on the committee. The reader should therefore check the body's remit, look for the reasoning rather than the conclusion, and note any connection between its members and the bidders.

questions.explanation: Weight should track the body's competence on the exact question, the transparency of its reasoning and its independence from the bidders. Naming a body without checking those three things borrows authority instead of evidence.
questions.hint: Ask whether the reasoning is published and who benefits.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What the crowd does as a reason
questions.learningObjective: Set the boundary of what a survey percentage can be taken to show
questions.stem: A proposal argues that most residents approve of the scheme because a survey found 62 per cent approval. Which judgement is soundest?

options.text: It shows approval among those surveyed, which is meaningful support but only as far as the sample and question allow
A 62 per cent result settles the question of majority opinion among residents generally
options.misconception: Assumes a 62 per cent result settles majority opinion

options.text: Poll percentages are worthless because people change their minds between the survey and the decision
options.misconception: Believes poll percentages are worthless because opinions shift

options.text: Approval of the scheme implies approval of every detail of its design, so no further consultation is needed
options.misconception: Treats approval of a scheme as approval of every design detail

questions.explanation: A survey result speaks for the people surveyed under the question asked, and it is real evidence of support within that frame. It cannot be stretched to the whole population or to the design in detail.
questions.hint: Ask who was asked and what was asked.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Sequence mistaken for cause
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a timeline order establishes and what it leaves open
questions.stem: Two steps: place the maintenance change and the improvement on a timeline. Then say what the order establishes.

options.text: The earlier event is thereby the established cause, so the report may close the enquiry
options.misconception: Assumes the earlier event is thereby the established cause

options.text: A timeline can never contribute anything to a causal case, so the report should not use it at all
options.misconception: Believes a timeline can never contribute to a causal case

options.text: The improvement proves the change was necessary, since nothing could have happened without it
options.misconception: Treats the improvement as proof the change was necessary

options.text: It establishes the improvement followed the change, making it a candidate explanation, not a demonstrated cause

questions.explanation: Order contributes a hypothesis and rules out explanations that would have had to act first, but it cannot rule out a common cause or an unrelated change that happened at the same time.
questions.hint: Ask what else could have begun in the same month.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Revising a claim so it can be answered
questions.learningObjective: Choose the direct measurement that would settle a physical claim
questions.stem: A report claims the new timetable will reduce crowding, and a member asks what would count as evidence that it did.

options.text: Passenger satisfaction ratings would show whether people found the new arrangement less crowded
options.misconception: Assumes satisfaction ratings are the natural measure to use

options.text: Measured crowding per train in the peak periods, compared with the same periods before the change
Evidence of any kind would settle it, since the direction of travel is what matters in the end
options.misconception: Believes evidence of any kind will settle a crowding claim

options.text: The absence of complaints about crowding would show the timetable has done what was promised
options.misconception: Treats the absence of complaints as the decisive indicator

questions.explanation: Crowding is a physical quantity, so the natural test measures it directly under comparable conditions, at comparable times, before and after. Opinions and complaint levels are indirect and can move for other reasons.
questions.hint: Ask what would be measured and against which baseline.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Two options presented as the whole field
questions.learningObjective: Read a minute for the scope of the decision it records

stimulus.body: The minute records the decision between the two proposals put forward by the assessment team. It does not record any other proposal that was considered, and the accompanying paper lists only those two options.

questions.stem: What can a reader safely conclude from this minute?

options.text: That the board chose between two options, and nothing at all about whether other options existed
That the board was given a complete set of choices, since the paper accompanying the minute is authoritative
options.misconception: Assumes the board was given a complete set of choices

options.text: That no other option existed, since a minute records every matter the board dealt with that day
options.misconception: Believes silence in the minute shows no other option existed

options.text: That the chosen option was the best one available, since the board selected it after debate
options.misconception: Treats the minute as evidence the chosen option was best

questions.explanation: The minute is a record of a decision between the options that were tabled, not of the range that existed. Silence about alternatives is a gap in the record rather than evidence that there were none.
questions.hint: Ask what the minute was about, and what it was not about.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Circular argument
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose a self-supporting business case and describe how to rebuild it
questions.stem: A business case says the depot is unnecessary because traffic has fallen, and that traffic has fallen because the depot is unnecessary. Explain the fault and how the case could be rebuilt.

answer.exemplar: The case is circular: the decline in traffic is offered as a reason to close the depot, and the closing of the depot is offered as the reason for the decline, so the document argues with itself and reaches no external evidence. To rebuild it, the depot's role must first be stated without assuming closure, so that the traffic figures can be examined for what they are: a trend across the network, the effect of route changes, seasonality, or the loss of journeys that once passed this depot.

questions.explanation: The two claims hold each other up, so the reader is given no independent ground on which to judge the closure. Setting out the depot's role before the traffic figures lets the figures be tested against other explanations.
questions.hint: Ask what the depot does before assuming it is not needed.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Generalising from too small a base
questions.learningObjective: Locate the real fault in a weak sample rather than in its size alone
questions.stem: A survey of 60 evening travellers is used to support a claim about the whole region's travel patterns. Which criticism is most precise?

options.text: A round number of respondents is itself suspicious, so the survey should be repeated with an odd figure
options.misconception: Assumes a round number of respondents is itself suspect

options.text: Regional claims need thousands of respondents by definition, whatever the survey's design quality
options.misconception: Believes regional claims always need thousands of respondents

options.text: Sixty evening travellers at one stop describe that group and hour, and cannot carry a regional claim
Evening travellers are a cross-section of all travellers by definition, so the sample is inherently fair
options.misconception: Treats evening travellers as a cross-section of all travellers

questions.explanation: The fault is not the count but the gap between what was sampled and what is claimed; sixty could support a narrow claim where a thousand would not support a broad one. The criticism should name that gap.
questions.hint: Ask what the sample covers and what the claim covers.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: When an appeal to authority holds
questions.learningObjective: Judge how far a decision by another authority carries to a local decision
questions.stem: Now identify what the cited document establishes and then judge what follows for the local decision.

options.text: Another authority's decision settles the local question, since the same legislation applies in both places
options.misconception: Assumes another authority's decision settles the local question

options.text: Citing any document at all makes the case rigorous, so the local board need only note the reference
options.misconception: Believes citing any document at all makes the case rigorous

options.text: The local board has no role once a precedent exists, since consistency is required for the network
options.misconception: Treats the local board as having no role once precedent exists

options.text: It establishes what another authority decided, so the local board must still judge whether those reasons apply here

questions.explanation: A cited decision supplies evidence about one case, and its value here depends on whether the facts behind it are shared. The board's job is to judge that, not to treat the precedent as self-applying.
questions.hint: Ask whether the reasons behind it hold locally.
